title: WETT Inspection In Ontario: Who Needs One & Why | Northmark
description: What a WETT inspection is, when your insurer or a home purchase requires one, the three inspection levels, and what happens if the chimney fails.
h1: WETT Inspection In Ontario: What It Is, Who Needs One, What To Expect
lead: If you are buying a house with a wood-burning fireplace or stove in Ontario, or your insurer has asked for it, you have probably heard the word WETT. Here is what it means, what the inspection actually covers, and how to get it done without being sold a chimney you do not need.

hero.alt: Brick chimney above the roofline, photographed during a Northmark inspection in Toronto

hero_caption: An inspection starts outside: the cap, the crown, the brick and the flashing — then the flue, from the top and from the firebox.

sections.body:
WETT stands for Wood Energy Technology Transfer. It is the non-profit body in Canada that trains and certifies people who install, inspect and sweep wood-burning systems: fireplaces, inserts, stoves and the chimneys that serve them. A WETT-certified technician has passed its courses and exams and holds a current certificate number.

A "WETT inspection" is an inspection of a wood-burning system carried out by a WETT-certified person, checking it against the installation code (CSA B365) and the manufacturer's clearances, and written up in a report.

• Insurance companies. Most Ontario insurers ask for a WETT inspection before they insure a home with a wood-burning fireplace or stove, and some ask for a new one when you renew or switch insurers. The report tells them the appliance is installed to code and the chimney is sound.
  • Home buyers. A home inspector looks at the fireplace, but usually does not certify it. If you are buying a house with a wood stove or fireplace, a WETT inspection before closing tells you whether you are inheriting a working system or a rebuild.
  • Homeowners who want to know. A fireplace that has not been used for years, a chimney with visible damage, a stove the previous owner installed — all reasons to have it checked before the first fire.

WETT defines three levels. The right one depends on why you need it.

  • Level 1 — Readily accessible. A visual check of everything that can be seen without tools or ladders: the appliance, its clearances to combustibles, the visible chimney, the cap, the connection. This is what most insurers ask for on an existing, unchanged installation.
  • Level 2 — Accessible. Everything in Level 1, plus the parts reached with ladders and basic tools: the chimney from the roof, the attic where the chimney passes through, the flue interior. Usually recommended when a home changes hands or an appliance has been changed.
  • Level 3 — Concealed. The parts that can only be reached by opening up walls or ceilings. Rare, and only called for when a Level 2 finds a problem that cannot be assessed without it.

On a fireplace, in plain terms:

  • The firebox and its lining, the damper, the smoke shelf and smoke chamber.
  • The flue: the liner, whether it is intact, whether it is the right size for the appliance, and whether anything is blocking it.
  • The chimney outside: the cap, the crown, the mortar joints, the flashing, and the height of the chimney above the roof.
  • Clearances: how far combustible materials — mantels, framing, trim — are from the firebox opening and from the chimney.
  • On a stove or insert: the clearances around the unit, the floor protection, and the chimney connection.

A proper inspection comes with photos. If your report has no photos of the flue, it was not looked at.

A "fail" is a list of deficiencies, not a verdict on the house. The common ones are fixable: a missing cap, a cracked crown, open joints, a damper that does not seat, a flue that needs a liner, a clearance problem at the mantel. The report says what has to be corrected; once it is, a re-inspection confirms it and the insurer gets the updated report.

Our approach: you get the photos and a written price for each item, separately, so you can decide what to fix now and what can wait — and you can take the report to anyone for a second opinion.

Our technician is WETT-certified. The standard inspection — 19 points inside and out, with photos — is free at your home anywhere in Toronto and the GTA. If your insurer or your lawyer needs a formal WETT report, say so when you book; we confirm what your insurer is asking for and what, if anything, it costs before we come. See chimney inspections.

faq.q: How long is a WETT inspection valid for?
faq.a: The report describes the system on the day it was inspected. Insurers set their own rules — many accept a report that is a few years old if nothing has changed, and ask for a new one when you switch insurers or change the appliance. Ask your broker what they will accept.

faq.q: Is a WETT inspection the same as a chimney sweep?
faq.a: No. The sweep removes soot and creosote; the inspection checks the system against the code. They are often done on the same visit, and a flue is easier to inspect once it is clean.

faq.q: Do I need a WETT inspection for a gas fireplace?
faq.a: No — WETT covers wood-burning systems. Gas appliances in Ontario fall under the TSSA and are inspected by a licensed gas technician. We can still inspect the chimney a gas fireplace vents through.

faq.q: Can you inspect a house I am about to buy?
faq.a: Yes. Book the inspection for a day you have access to the house, and tell us it is a purchase — we photograph everything and give you the report and the prices in writing, so you know what you are buying before you close.
